title: Line up two clocks
briefing: auditd stamps events in Unix epoch seconds. sar prints a 12-hour clock with AM and PM. Neither looks like the other, and neither looks like syslog.
Put the dropper's start and the first sign of load on the same clock. That gap is how long the host ran the attacker's job before anything was measurable.

lesson.p: Two formats that break naive pipelines. `sar -u` prints space-aligned columns with the time split across two fields (`11:30:01` and `PM`). auditd writes `msg=audit(1773443985.897:18131)`: seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, milliseconds, and a serial number. GNU `date` converts both.

flags: sar data rows: awk's default splitting handles the padding, so field 1 is the time, 2 is AM/PM, 3 is CPU, 4 is %user
stop awk at the first match: "the first sample where..."
epoch seconds to a readable UTC time
a readable time to epoch seconds, which sort numerically across formats
split on `(` or `.`, so field 2 of an audit line is the epoch

lesson.note: 12 AM is midnight and 12 PM is noon, so `12:10:01 AM` comes before `01:00:01 AM`. Sorting a 12-hour clock as text puts every PM sample in the wrong place. Convert to 24-hour (or epoch) first, then sort.
Use `date -u` for epochs. Without it, `date` prints in the local timezone: this VM is UTC, but your RHEL laptop or a server in another region may not be.

stages.why: Data rows have `all` in the CPU column. The header has `CPU` there, and the Average line has `all` in field 2, so both are skipped.
Time, AM/PM, and %user. No `tr -s` needed: awk's default separator is any run of spaces.

examples.title: The first sample over a threshold

stages.why: Print the time and stop: only the first crossing matters.

examples.title: Pull the epoch out of audit records

stages.why: The separator is a character class: `(` or `.`. The epoch sits between `audit(` and the first `.`.
Field 2. The two last lines share an epoch: one SYSCALL and its EXECVE describe the same event, and the serial after the `:` (803) proves it.

examples.title: Epoch to readable time
examples.command: awk -F'[(.]' '{print $2}' training/audit.log | while read -r e; do date -u -d "@$e" '+%F %T'; done

stages.why: Run `date` once per epoch. `-r` keeps backslashes literal; a habit worth having.
`@` means seconds since the epoch; `-u` prints UTC.

examples.title: Check sar's Average against your own
examples.command: awk '$2 ~ /AM|PM/ && $3 == "all" {s += $4; n++} END {printf "%.2f\n", s / n}' training/sar.txt; awk '/^Average/ {print $3}' training/sar.txt

stages.why: On the Average line the columns shift left by one (no AM/PM), so %user is field 3. The two numbers agree, which proves you parsed the right column.

challenge.question: When did the dropper start (the timestamp of its EXECVE record in var/log/audit/audit.log), and what is the time of the first sample in metrics/sar_cpu.txt whose %user is above 50? Give both in 24-hour UTC.
challenge.format: Two times as HH:MM:SS separated by one space, dropper first, for example 08:15:00 08:20:01

hints: Two lookups, then two conversions. The dropper's record is the one with `--pool` in it. In sar, `%user` is field 4 on data rows, and the first match is enough.

Epoch: `grep -- --pool` the audit log, then cut the number out of `audit(...)`, then `date -u -d @EPOCH +%T`. sar: `awk '$3 == "all" && $4 > 50 {print $1, $2; exit}'`, then `date -d 'HH:MM:SS PM' +%T`.
e=$(grep -- --pool var/log/audit/audit.log | awk -F'[(.]' '{print $2}'); s=$(awk '$3 == "all" && $4 > 50 {print $1, $2; exit}' metrics/sar_cpu.txt); echo "$(date -u -d @$e +%T) $(date -d "$s" +%___)"

debrief.solution: e=$(grep -- --pool var/log/audit/audit.log | awk -F'[(.]' '{print $2}'); s=$(awk '$3 == "all" && $4 > 50 {print $1, $2; exit}' metrics/sar_cpu.txt); echo "$(date -u -d @$e +%T) $(date -d "$s" +%T)"
debrief.alternative: echo $(date -u -d @$(sed -n 's/.*audit(\([0-9]*\)\..*a1="--pool".*/\1/p' var/log/audit/audit.log) +%T; awk '$3 == "all" && $4 > 50 {print $1, $2; exit}' metrics/sar_cpu.txt | xargs -I{} date -d {} +%T)
why: The dropper started at 23:19:45 and the first sar sample over 50% is 23:30:01. sar samples every 10 minutes, so all it can tell you is that the load began somewhere between 23:20:01 and 23:30:01. The 5-minute metrics in Level 6 narrow that, and auditd gives the exact second. That is why you correlate sources: each one has a different resolution.

On RHEL, `sar -u -f /var/log/sa/sa13` reads the same data, and running it as `LC_ALL=C sar ...` prints a 24-hour clock, because sar takes its time format from the locale. Asking sar for the format you want is easier than converting AM and PM afterwards.

`ausearch -i --start '03/13/2026 23:00:00'` filters and decodes audit records by time on a live host. The epoch is still worth knowing: you will meet it in journald (`__REALTIME_TIMESTAMP`), cron logs, and most JSON logs.
